summary: This extension to SIP event notification lets a subscriber subscribe to an entire homogeneous list of resources instead of sending a SUBSCRIBE for each one. The subscriber is then notified when the state of any resource in the list changes.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4662 extends SIP notifications so a client can ask about a list of resources in one go instead of one subscription per resource. A server called the resource list server keeps the list, subscribes to each resource on the client's behalf, and sends back a single message that carries the state of everything on the list. The RFC also explains how the client and the server agree that the extension is supported, and what has to be done about authentication.

subtitle: Lets a SIP client subscribe to a whole list of resources at once and be told when any of them changes.

tldr.problem: A SIP client that wants to know about several resources has to send a separate subscription for each one, and each notifier may then insist on its own refresh interval and its own rate of updates. On a narrow link that is a lot of traffic the client did not ask for.
tldr.mechanism: A resource list server holds the list. The client sends one SUBSCRIBE for the list, and the server subscribes to each resource on its own behalf, with back-end subscriptions, and then sends the client one notification carrying the state of every resource. Each notification body is a multipart document whose root part is an XML document describing the list and pointing at the parts that carry the state.
tldr.outcome: The result is one subscription and one stream of updates for a whole list, with the server free to batch and rate-limit the changes. The RFC also sets out the security consequences of a server acting on the client's behalf, including the risk of showing one user's state to another.

today: RFC 4662 is a Proposed Standard from August 2006 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It extends the SIP event notification mechanism of RFC 3265, and it asks IANA to register a SIP option tag, a media type and an XML namespace. The authenticated identity mechanism it relies on for back-end subscriptions is RFC 4474.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The SIP-specific event notification mechanism lets a user, the subscriber, ask to be told about changes in the state of a particular resource. The subscriber sends a SUBSCRIBE request for the resource, and a notifier that represents the resource processes it.

Often a subscriber has a list of resources it is interested in. Without an aggregating mechanism, the subscriber has to send a SUBSCRIBE for each resource. In environments where bandwidth is limited, such as wireless networks, that is problematic. It generates substantial message traffic, in the form of the initial SUBSCRIBE requests and the refreshes of each individual subscription. The notifier may insist on low refresh intervals, in order to avoid a long-lived subscription state, so the subscriber may have to refresh faster than it would like or has the capacity to. And the notifier may generate NOTIFY requests more rapidly than the subscriber wants, causing more traffic than the subscriber asked for.

This specification defines an extension to the event notification mechanism of RFC 3265 that allows notifications for lists of resources to be requested and conveyed. A resource list is identified by a URI and represents a list of zero or more URIs, each of which identifies an individual resource for which the subscriber wants information. In many cases the URI that identifies the list will be a SIP URI, but the use of other schemes, such as pres:, is also foreseen.

The notifier for the list is called a resource list server, or RLS. In order to determine the state of the entire list, the resource list server acts as if it has generated a subscription to each resource in the list.

The resource list is not restricted to being inside the domain of the subscriber, and the resources in the list are not constrained to be in the domain of the resource list server.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP lets a program ask to be told when the state of a resource changes, one resource at a time. This RFC lets it ask about a whole list instead and receive one stream of updates for the list. A server called the resource list server does the subscribing on the client's behalf.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The document defines a small set of terms that carry most of its meaning.

A list subscription is a subscription to a resource list, and in list subscriptions the resource list server acts as the notifier. A back-end subscription is any subscription, SIP or otherwise, that the resource list server creates to learn the state of a resource. The server creates back-end subscriptions for resources about which it is not the authority, and for them the server acts as the subscriber.

A resource is any logical entity that has a state, or states, that can be subscribed to, and resources are identified by URIs. A resource list is a list of zero or more resources whose individual states can be subscribed to with a single subscription.

A virtual subscription is a logical construct within a resource list server that represents the subscriptions to the resources in a resource list. For each list subscription it services, the server creates at least one virtual subscription for every resource in that list. When the server is not the authority for the state of a resource, the virtual subscription is associated with a back-end subscription; when it is the authority, the virtual subscription has no corresponding back-end subscription.

RLMI, Resource List Meta-Information, is a document that describes the state of the virtual subscriptions associated with a list subscription.
sections.plainLanguage: Three roles matter: the client that subscribes, the server that holds the list and does the subscribing on the client's behalf, and the servers that actually know each resource's state. The document gives names to the subscriptions the list server makes on its own behalf, and to the document that describes them.

sections.title: Overview of Operation
sections.content:
The first step is the creation of a resource list, represented by a SIP URI. The list contains a set of URIs, each representing a resource for which the subscriber wants to receive information, and it can exist in any domain. The list could be manipulated through a web page, a voice response system or some other protocol; the specific means by which the list is created and maintained is outside the scope of this specification.

To learn the resource state of the elements on the list, the user sends a single SUBSCRIBE request targeted at the URI of the list. This is routed to a resource list server for that URI. The server acts as a notifier, authenticates the subscriber, and accepts the subscription.

The server may have direct information about some or all of the resources specified by the list. If it does not, it can subscribe to the non-local resources in the list. Such subscriptions may or may not be SIP subscriptions; any mechanism for determining such information may be employed, and the document uses the term back-end subscription for all of them.

As the state of resources in the list changes, the server generates notifications to the list subscribers. It can, at its discretion, buffer notifications of resource changes and send the resource information to the subscriber in batches rather than individually, which allows it to provide rate limiting for the subscriber.

The list notifications contain a body of type multipart/related. The root section of the multipart/related content is an XML document that provides meta-information about each resource present in the list, and the remaining sections contain the actual state information for each resource.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends one subscription request for the list, and the list server replies with notifications that carry the state of every resource on the list. The server can bundle several changes into one notification, which also lets it slow the updates down to a rate the client can manage.

sections.title: Negotiating Support and Subscription Duration
sections.content:
The extension uses the SIP option tag mechanism to negotiate support for it. Any client that supports the event list extension includes the option tag eventlist in a Supported header field of every SUBSCRIBE message for a subscription for which it is willing to process a list. If the subscription is made to a URI that represents a list, the server includes eventlist in a Require header field of the response to the SUBSCRIBE, and in all NOTIFY messages within that subscription, because the NOTIFY would not be usable without applying the extension.

Putting Require: eventlist in a SUBSCRIBE request serves no purpose except to break interoperability in certain cases, and is consequently not recommended. Sending Supported: eventlist in a NOTIFY message is meaningless, and implementations should not include it in any request except for SUBSCRIBE.

There is nothing in a SIP URI that indicates whether it represents a list of resources or a single resource. If a subscriber sends a request to a URI that represents a list resource but does not include a Supported header field listing the eventlist token, the notifier will typically return a 421 Extension Required response. The SIP specification advises that servers avoid returning 421 and instead attempt to process the request without the extension, but in this case the URI fundamentally represents a list resource, and therefore the subscription cannot proceed without this extension.

Since the primary benefit of the resource list server is to reduce the overall messaging volume to a subscriber, it is recommended that the subscription duration for a list be reasonably long. The default, when no duration is specified, is taken from the underlying event package, and the standard techniques of the event notification specification can be used to increase or reduce it.

An implementation compliant with this specification must support the multipart/related and application/rlmi+xml media types, and must include them in an Accept header sent in a SUBSCRIBE message, in addition to any other types supported by the client, including the types required by the event package being used.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says in its subscription request that it understands lists, and the server says the same in its reply and in every update. If the client does not say so, the server normally refuses with a 421 rather than guessing.

sections.title: The RLMI Document and Its Parts
sections.content:
To convey the state of multiple resources, the list extension uses the multipart/related media type. The root document of the multipart body must be a Resource List Meta-Information document, of the type application/rlmi+xml, holding the meta-information for the resources in the notification.

The document has four elements. A list element holds the information about the list as a whole and carries three mandatory attributes. The uri attribute holds the URI that corresponds to the list, typically the URI the SUBSCRIBE request was sent to. The version attribute holds a number from 0 to 2^32-1, which must be 0 for the first NOTIFY message sent within a subscription and must increase by exactly one for each subsequent NOTIFY sent within that subscription. The fullState attribute says whether the NOTIFY contains information for every resource in the list; the first NOTIFY sent in a subscription must contain full state, as must the first NOTIFY sent after receipt of a SUBSCRIBE request. A cid attribute may also be present, identifying a section within the multipart body that contains aggregate state for the resources in the list.

Each resource element corresponds to a resource being reported in the notification and must carry the uri attribute that identifies it, typically a SIP URI that, if subscribed to, would return the state of that resource. Each resource element holds zero or more instance elements, which represent a single notifier for the resource. For event packages that allow forking, multiple virtual subscriptions may exist for a given resource, and they are represented as multiple instance elements; where forking does not occur, at most one instance is present.

An instance carries an id, an opaque string used to identify the instance uniquely within its resource, whose construction is an implementation decision. It carries a state of active, pending or terminated, with the same meanings as the Subscription-State header field of the event notification specification. When the state is terminated a reason attribute must also be present, with the same values as the reason parameter of that header field, though the subscriber is not expected to take automated action on it. Finally, the cid attribute, which must be present when the state is active, identifies the section of the multipart body that contains the actual resource state, expressed in the content type the event package defines for state.

Lists and resources may also carry name elements with human-readable names, each optionally carrying the standard XML language attribute so that an application can decide which of several names to show. Because a cid attribute may refer only to top-level parts of the multipart document, a nested list brings its own RLMI document, and the parts inside it are referenced from that document instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Each update carries a small XML document that says which resources the update is about and, for each, whether the list server is watching it, waiting to watch it, or has stopped. The actual state of each resource travels in a separate part of the same message, and the XML document points at it.

sections.title: Constructing Coherent Resource State
sections.content:
The subscriber maintains a table for each resource list. The table contains a row for each resource in the list, indexed by the URI of that resource, taken from the uri attribute of each resource element, and the contents of each row hold the state of that resource as conveyed in the resource document. For resources that provide versioning information, which the event notification specification mandates for any format that allows partial notification, each row also holds a resource state version number, initialized with the version specified in the first document received and used when comparing versions of partial notifications.

How a notification is processed depends on whether it contains full or partial state. A full state notification is checked against the local version number first: if the version attribute in the received message is not greater than the local version number, the received document is discarded without any further processing. Otherwise the contents of the resource list table are flushed and repopulated from the document, with a new row for each resource element.

For a partial state notification, the version numbers are compared to check that no list notifications have been lost. If the value in the new document is exactly one higher than the local version number, the local version number is increased by one and the document is processed. If it is more than one higher, the local version number is set to the value in the new document and the subscriber should also generate a refresh request to trigger a full state notification. If the version in the document is less than or equal to the local version, the document is discarded without any further processing.

For each resource listed in the document, the subscriber checks whether a row exists, comparing the resource URI with the URI associated with the row. If the resource is not in the table, a row is added and its state set from the resource element; if it is, its state is updated as the event package defines. A row whose state has become terminated may be removed from the table at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: The client keeps a table of the state of every resource on the list. Each update carries a version number, and the client discards an update that is older than what it already has, or that has skipped versions, in which case it asks for a full update instead. A full update replaces the whole table; a partial one changes only the resources it names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanisms for obtaining state information for resources in a list are generally left to the implementor, and the security issues below are specific to the circumstance in which a SIP back-end subscription is used for that purpose. Implementors using other mechanisms must analyse their chosen access methods for the relevant security issues themselves.

Authentication is the first concern. When back-end subscriptions are required to retrieve resource state information, the end user is no longer the direct subscriber to the state of the resource, so direct authentication of the user is no longer possible. The most common deployment is for the subscribers of a list server to be in the same domain as the server, and in that case the server has the ability to act as an authentication service. It authenticates the subscriber and then includes an Identity header field in all of the back-end subscriptions it performs on behalf of that authenticated user, cryptographically asserting that the request is authorized to be made on behalf of the user in the From header field. Any list server that uses SIP back-end subscriptions to acquire information about the resources in a resource list must be able to act as an authentication service, provided that local administrative policy allows it.

When the subscriber and the list server are in different domains, the authenticated identity extensions give the server no means to vouch for the user's identity, and general solutions are left for future study. Until they are developed, a list server in a different domain should subscribe to the resources using its own identity, which will generally obtain only the resource information that is made publicly available. A client may instead attempt direct subscriptions to the resources named in the uri attribute of the resource elements in the RLMI document, which allows proper authentication of the user and will generally authorise it to receive more complete state information; such a client should use the data it retrieved that way instead of the list information.

Improper aggregation is the second concern. A list server typically serves several subscribers at once, the same resource may be present in several lists, and two users may subscribe to the same list. In these cases a misguided implementation may try to reduce the network load by keeping only one back-end subscription to a resource and presenting the result to more than one user, which circumvents the authorization policy of the notifier. Authorization is often much more than a simple allowed or not allowed decision, because resources may render very different, and even conflicting, states depending on the identity of the subscribing user. Implementations must not present the result of one back-end subscription to more than one user unless the server has adequate access to the complete authorization policy of the resource and can and has determined that presenting the information to more than one user does not violate that policy. The document notes that this is a very difficult problem to solve correctly, and that even where it seems possible the mode of operation is not recommended.

On signing and sealing, any section of the MIME body may be signed or encrypted as necessary. A list server should take care not to modify the MIME bodies it receives from back-end subscriptions, and should not generally rely on being able to read them. It should pass along its support for multipart/signed and application/pkcs7-mime to any SIP back-end subscriptions if the subscriber included those types in the initial SUBSCRIBE, because failing to do so may make a resource refuse to divulge its state, or make the subscriber discard valid state. Actually encrypting or signing the bodies is not necessary in order to pass them through.

Nesting lists creates a last risk: the ability to nest resource lists makes it possible to create lists that contain themselves as a sub-list. When back-end subscriptions are created to service virtual subscriptions, that can become an infinite loop of subscriptions. Implementors of list servers that create back-end subscriptions must implement safeguards to prevent it, and applying filters to the back-end subscriptions is an effective way to preclude the problem.
sections.plainLanguage: When a list server subscribes to the resources on your behalf, it is no longer you who is authenticated, so the RFC says how the server must prove whose requests it is making. It also warns against sharing one subscription's results between several users, because what a resource shows often depends on who is asking, and against lists that contain themselves.

messages.label: SUBSCRIBE
messages.note: One subscription for the whole list, with Supported: eventlist and the Accept types for rlmi+xml and multipart/related.

messages.label: 200 OK
messages.note: The server accepts the subscription and answers with Require: eventlist.

messages.label: SUBSCRIBE
messages.note: A back-end subscription for a resource the list server is not the authority for.

messages.label: SUBSCRIBE
messages.note: A back-end subscription for a second, non-local resource.

messages.label: NOTIFY
messages.note: The state of every resource on the list in one multipart/related body, whose root part is the RLMI document.

root.label: list
root.note: Attributes: uri, version, fullState, and an optional cid

children.label: name
children.note: Human-readable name, with an optional xml:lang

cells: Discard the document unless its version is greater than the local one
Exactly one higher is processed; more than one higher sets the local version and should trigger a refresh; lower or equal is discarded
The table is flushed and repopulated from the document
Only the resources named in the document are added or updated, and the others are left as they are
The first NOTIFY in a subscription must carry full state
Later notifications may carry partial state

items.label: active
items.desc: The virtual subscription is in place. The cid attribute must be present and points at the part holding the state.

items.label: pending
items.desc: The subscription is not yet in place, and no state is carried for it.

items.label: terminated
items.desc: The virtual subscription has ended. A reason attribute must be present.
